opts.t: Deep to transverse process in paravertebral space

Intramuscular placement is not the interfascial ESP target and may give inconsistent spread.

questions.expl: An ESP catheter lies in the fascial plane between erector spinae and the transverse processes; advancing several centimetres in-plane facilitates longitudinal spread.

opts.why: Laryngeal adductors recover relatively quickly and are less susceptible than pharyngeal muscles to residual weakness.
The diaphragm is relatively resistant to non-depolarising blockade, not the most sensitive group.
Abdominal muscles are not as sensitive as pharyngeal dilators to clinically significant residual blockade.

questions.expl: Pharyngeal muscles are particularly vulnerable to residual neuromuscular blockade; the diaphragm is comparatively resistant. Recalled banks disagree because adductor pollicis is used as a recovery monitoring surrogate.

questions.stem: The most common cause of mortality in children with diabetic ketoacidosis is

opts.why: Hypoglycaemia is a preventable treatment complication, but cerebral injury is the classic leading fatal complication of paediatric DKA.
Cerebral venous thrombosis is uncommon and does not account for the largest proportion of DKA deaths.
Acute kidney injury occurs with dehydration but is not the characteristic leading cause of death.

questions.expl: Cerebral injury, classically cerebral oedema, is a major cause of DKA-related paediatric death and must be monitored during treatment.

questions.stem: The intubating dose of atracurium in a patient with post-polio syndrome should be

opts.why: A doubled dose risks prolonged paralysis in patients with increased sensitivity after poliomyelitis.

opts.t: A routine 0.5 mg/kg dose without monitoring
opts.why: A conventional dose without quantitative monitoring ignores individual variability and the possibility of prolonged block.
A fixed adult bolus is inappropriate without reference to weight, response and residual neuromuscular function.

opts.t: A substantially reduced, titrated dose (recalled 0.05 mg/kg)

questions.expl: Post-polio patients may have increased sensitivity to nondepolarising block. Use individual titration and quantitative monitoring rather than an unmodified standard dose.
questions.note: The 0.05 mg/kg figure is recalled but not a universally validated intubating dose; clinical management requires titration.

questions.stem: In the morbidly obese the induction dose of propofol should be calculated based on

opts.why: Total body weight can substantially overdose the induction bolus because adipose mass does not proportionally increase initial central drug requirements.
Ideal body weight alone may underestimate the lean-tissue distribution component; dose is titrated to effect.

opts.t: Adjusted body weight with a fixed 40% correction
opts.why: A fixed adjusted-weight formula is not the standard recalled method for the induction bolus.

questions.expl: Propofol induction is commonly based on lean body weight in morbid obesity with titration to effect. Total-body-weight dosing risks excessive induction dose.

questions.stem: All of the following conditions are associated with acromegaly EXCEPT

opts.why: Growth-hormone excess produces insulin resistance and glucose intolerance, making diabetes an association.
Hypertension is common from sodium retention, vascular effects and associated OSA.
OSA is strongly associated with soft-tissue overgrowth and upper-airway narrowing.

opts.t: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease as a direct association

questions.expl: Acromegaly commonly causes sleep-disordered breathing, insulin resistance/diabetes and hypertension; COPD itself is not a characteristic direct manifestation.

questions.stem: The composition of blood returned to the patient from intraoperative cell salvage shows

opts.why: A washed red-cell product does not deliberately remove RBC 2,3-DPG; oxygen-carrying RBCs remain.

opts.t: Whole blood with normal clotting factors
opts.why: Cell salvage removes most plasma and clotting factors, so the product is not whole blood.
Platelets are largely washed away; it is not a platelet concentrate.

opts.t: A concentrated red-cell suspension with preserved 2,3-DPG and little plasma/platelets

questions.expl: Washed cell salvage produces red cells at roughly 50–70% haematocrit while removing much plasma, platelets and clotting factors. RBC 2,3-DPG is relatively preserved.

The radial nerve lies deep/posterior to the artery, not in the separate muscular interval shown.

questions.stem: Severe obstructive sleep apnoea in a 6-year-old child is confirmed if during polysomnography the apnoea/hypopnea index (AHI) is greater than or equal to

opts.why: An obstructive AHI of at least 1 is abnormal in children but defines any OSA, not severe disease.
An AHI of 5 typically represents moderate paediatric OSA, not the conventional severe threshold.
Thirty events per hour is the severe adult threshold, not the usual paediatric definition.

questions.expl: Common paediatric criteria define severe OSA at obstructive AHI ≥10/hour; adult severity boundaries are different (severe ≥30/hour).

questions.stem: Predictors of successful awake extubation after volatile anaesthesia in infants include

opts.t: A fixed spontaneous tidal volume without arousal
opts.why: Tidal volume without return of consciousness or protective reflexes does not establish awake-extubation readiness.
An isolated limb movement can be a reflex and is less predictive of purposeful arousal.

opts.t: A grimace in the absence of other signs
opts.why: Facial grimacing alone is nonspecific and does not prove coordinated airway protection.

opts.t: Purposeful movement and coordinated conjugate gaze

questions.expl: Awake extubation readiness depends on recovery of airway protection and appropriate purposeful responses, not one isolated motor sign.
questions.note: Study-derived extubation indicators vary; use clinician assessment rather than this isolated checklist.

questions.stem: Major international guidelines recommend maintaining the core body temperature between 32°C and 36°C in comatose patients after

opts.why: Temperature-control guidance concerns hypoxic brain injury after cardiac arrest, not uncomplicated volume loss.
Routine elective cardiac surgery without post-arrest coma is not this indication.

opts.t: Cardiac arrest with persistent coma after ROSC

opts.why: An isolated postoperative fever warrants evaluation and treatment, not routine induction of 32–36°C hypothermia.

questions.expl: At the time of this paper, post-resuscitation temperature control of 32–36°C was recommended in unconscious survivors of cardiac arrest. Later recommendations emphasise fever prevention.
questions.note: Historical 2021 temperature guidance; recommendations subsequently evolved.

questions.stem: A man presents with a fractured tibia. He has increasing pain in his leg, loss of sensation on the plantar surface of his foot and weakness of toe flexion. This is most consistent with a compartment syndrome of the leg in the

opts.why: The lateral compartment affects fibular muscles and superficial fibular nerve, favouring dorsum-foot deficits.
The superficial posterior compartment houses gastrocnemius/soleus, not the deep toe flexors and tibial nerve.
The anterior compartment contains dorsiflexors/deep fibular nerve; expect dorsiflexion and first-web-space deficits.

questions.expl: The deep posterior tibial compartment contains the tibial nerve and long toe flexors, explaining plantar sensory loss and weak toe flexion.

questions.stem: The coagulopathy that can result from intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is due to

opts.t: Vitamin K deficiency causing reduced factors II, VII, IX and X

opts.why: Factor VIII is not vitamin-K dependent and is not selectively depleted by cholestatic vitamin K malabsorption.
Splenic platelet sequestration is unrelated to the characteristic fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.
Primary fibrinolysis is not the usual mechanism of cholestatic pregnancy coagulopathy.

questions.expl: Cholestasis impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K, leading to deficiency of vitamin-K-dependent coagulation factors.

questions.stem: The best patient position to evaluate the gastric contents with ultrasound is

Left-lateral positioning does not pool gastric fluid into the antrum as reliably as right lateral.
Prone positioning is neither standard nor as sensitive for gastric-antral volume assessment.

questions.expl: The right lateral position promotes fluid pooling in the dependent gastric antrum and increases ultrasound sensitivity for residual gastric content.

Vitamin B12 deficiency typically produces macrocytosis rather than low-ferritin microcytosis.

SVT is rarely the primary arrest rhythm and often retains a pulse.
Pulseless VT is possible but is not the most commonly reported initial maternal arrest rhythm.

questions.expl: Maternal arrest is often associated with hypoxia, haemorrhage or embolic causes and PEA is frequently the presenting non-shockable rhythm.

Cefazolin is a surgical prophylactic drug and not routinely indicated for IUD insertion.

Older age is associated with decreased haemodynamic reserve and severe BCIS.

PDA occlusion affects the inferior/posterior wall, rather than widespread anterior precordial leads.

Right lower-zone consolidation would lie on the opposite side and lacks classic lobar volume loss.

Volatile anaesthetics depress SSEP amplitude and prolong latency more substantially than nondepolarising blockade.

questions.stem: Toxicity of methylene blue is likely to be seen after single bolus dose (in mg/kg) greater than

opts.why: Three mg/kg exceeds standard vasoplegia doses but is not the cited threshold at which marked toxicity becomes likely.
One mg/kg is within typical clinical dosing, not a toxic threshold.
Two mg/kg is within the usual single-bolus treatment range.

questions.expl: Methylene blue vasoplegia dosing is typically 1–2 mg/kg; high cumulative/bolus doses around 7 mg/kg increase toxicity, including impaired oxygen transport and pulmonary effects.

questions.stem: A woman is having a potentially curative primary breast cancer resection. Compared with a sevoflurane and opioid technique, using a regional anaesthesia-analgesia technique with paravertebral block and a propofol infusion will result in

opts.why: The randomised trial showed no improvement in neuropathic pain at six months with the proposed regional/TIVA technique.
The trial found no significant difference in cancer recurrence.

opts.t: No significant reduction in cancer recurrence or persistent breast pain
Lower persistent incisional pain at 12 months
opts.why: Persistent incisional pain at twelve months was not significantly reduced by that approach.

questions.expl: The Sessler randomised trial found no reduction in recurrence, chronic incisional pain, or neuropathic pain with paravertebral/propofol versus sevoflurane/opioid anaesthesia.
questions.note: Original recalled options sometimes contain only false positive claims; includes evidence-based none-of-these option.

questions.stem: A normal 75 kg term parturient may be expected to have a total blood volume of

opts.why: 4.5 L approximates non-pregnant blood volume and ignores gestational expansion.
5 L underestimates the physiological blood-volume increase near term.
6 L accounts for some expansion but falls below the approximate 100 mL/kg estimate for this patient.

questions.expl: Term pregnancy expands blood volume; an often quoted estimate is ~100 mL/kg at term, giving about 7.5 L in a 75 kg parturient.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing robotic prostatectomy with controlled mandatory volume ventilation has the following measurements: (plateau pressure, PEEP, autoPEEP, peak pressure, tidal volume given) The static compliance is

opts.why: Forty results from using an inappropriate smaller pressure gradient, rather than plateau minus total PEEP.
Twenty miscalculates the driving pressure; the correct denominator is 32−(8+4)=20 cmH₂O.
Twenty-five follows an incorrect pressure correction and does not match 600/20.

questions.expl: Static compliance = 600 mL/(plateau 32 − total PEEP 12 cmH₂O) = 30 mL/cmH₂O. Include auto-PEEP; exclude peak airway pressure.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old professional athlete who underwent a knee arthroscopy under general anaesthesia becomes tachycardic in the recovery room. His non-invasive systolic blood pressure is 90 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG is obtained. The most appropriate therapy is

opts.why: Empirical beta-blockade risks hypotension and is unnecessary before attempting vagal measures in stable SVT.

opts.t: Adenosine 6 mg before any vagal attempt
opts.why: Adenosine is an appropriate next step after vagal manoeuvres, not generally the first measure.
Unsynchronised shock is for VF/pulseless VT, not a stable perfusing SVT.

opts.t: Valsalva manoeuvre for a stable regular SVT

questions.expl: In a conscious patient with a regular narrow-complex SVT and no signs of shock, a modified Valsalva manoeuvre is a first-line treatment; adenosine follows if it fails.
questions.note: Original ECG unavailable; remembered options favour Valsalva. True haemodynamic instability would instead favour synchronised cardioversion.

questions.stem: A patient requiring an elective joint replacement has had a recent stroke. The minimum time to wait after the stroke before proceeding with surgery is

opts.why: Two weeks is substantially shorter than contemporaneous post-stroke elective-surgery guidance.

opts.t: At least 6 months, preferably 9 months (2021 AHA/ASA advice)

opts.why: Four weeks remains too early for the minimum delay advised in the 2021 statement.
Twenty-four hours is inappropriate for non-urgent surgery following an acute stroke.

questions.expl: The contemporaneous AHA/ASA statement suggested delaying elective noncardiac surgery at least six months and possibly nine months. The recalled nine months is preferable rather than a strict minimum.
questions.note: 2024–2026 guidance is shorter (three months); this is explicitly a period-specific reconstruction.

questions.stem: The direct physiological effects of electroconvulsive therapy include

opts.t: An initial parasympathetic bradycardia followed by sympathetic tachycardia and hypertension

opts.why: ECT causes characteristic autonomic phases, including marked haemodynamic changes.

opts.t: Persistent vagal hypotension without catecholamine surge
opts.why: A catecholamine surge follows the initial vagal phase, so hypotension is not the only effect.
Bradycardia is brief; the later sympathetic tachycardia and hypertension cannot be ignored.

questions.expl: ECT produces a brief parasympathetic phase followed by a catecholamine surge, which commonly causes tachycardia and hypertension.

Pneumonia produces parenchymal opacification without marked mediastinal shift from pressurised pleural air.
The laterality is wrong and a simple pneumothorax lacks tension-associated displacement.

questions.stem: A common electrolyte disturbance following the administration of ferric carboxymaltose is

opts.why: Sodium concentration is not the characteristic FGF23-mediated complication of ferric carboxymaltose.
The iron formulation promotes phosphate wasting, not elevated plasma phosphate.
Magnesium elevation is not its characteristic biochemical effect.

questions.expl: Ferric carboxymaltose may raise intact FGF23 and induce renal phosphate wasting, causing hypophosphataemia.

questions.stem: Globe perforation during eye block is more common in myopic eyes because

opts.why: Myopia tends to elongate rather than shorten globe axial diameter.
Anterior chamber depth alone does not explain increased risk to the posterior sclera.
Vitreous volume is not characteristically reduced in the enlarged myopic globe.

opts.t: A longer axial globe length, especially with posterior staphyloma

questions.expl: High myopia enlarges and elongates the globe, bringing vulnerable posterior sclera into the trajectory of a needle block.

questions.stem: A five-year-old child weighing 25 kg is to be strictly nil by mouth overnight following a laparotomy. The most appropriate fluid prescription is

opts.t: 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose, approximately 45 mL/h
0.9% sodium chloride without glucose at 100 mL/h
opts.why: 100 mL/h is far above reduced postoperative maintenance for 25 kg and omits glucose in a fasting child.
Hypotonic saline increases hospital-acquired hyponatraemia risk during postoperative ADH secretion.
Glucose water provides inadequate sodium and risks dangerous hyponatraemia.

questions.expl: For a postoperative 25 kg child, isotonic maintenance with glucose and reduced rate (roughly two-thirds calculated maintenance) limits hyponatraemia risk during postoperative ADH excess.
questions.note: Use local postoperative fluid prescription/monitoring guidance; exact rate is a recalled exam option.

questions.stem: A four-year-old boy with a history of waddling gait, larger than normal calves and frequent falls receives a spontaneously breathing volatile-based anaesthetic with sevoflurane. One hour into the case he develops peaked T waves and then the end-tidal CO2 begins to rise. The most appropriate immediate treatment is to

opts.t: Stop sevoflurane, give IV calcium and urgently treat hyperkalaemia
Give dantrolene alone and ignore ECG hyperkalaemia
opts.why: Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, but this Duchenne presentation suggests rhabdomyolysis with immediately lethal hyperkalaemia.

opts.why: Bicarbonate alone does not stabilise hyperkalaemic myocardium or stop the triggering volatile exposure.
Continued volatile exposure can worsen anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia.

questions.expl: Duchenne muscular dystrophy can develop anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis with life-threatening hyperkalaemia; peaked T waves call for immediate calcium and resuscitation as well as stopping trigger.
questions.note: Rising ETCO₂ also raises concern for malignant hyperthermia; simultaneous MH algorithm may be warranted. Recalled options are ambiguous.

questions.stem: The substance that should be avoided in a patient with history of anaphylaxis to MMR vaccine is

opts.why: Normal saline contains no gelatin antigen and is not specifically contraindicated.

Ringer's lactate is crystalloid, not a gelatin-derived product.

questions.expl: MMR vaccine can contain gelatin; true gelatin anaphylaxis raises concern for gelatin-containing colloids, not every intravenous fluid.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of hereditary angiooedema requires an appendectomy for acute appendicitis. The most effective therapy for the prevention of an acute attack in the perioperative period is

opts.why: Tranexamic acid is less reliable as perioperative prophylaxis for bradykinin-mediated hereditary angioedema.
Adrenaline is not effective prophylaxis for C1 inhibitor deficiency, unlike for histamine-mediated anaphylaxis.
FFP contains C1 inhibitor but also attack-triggering substrates and is a fallback when concentrate unavailable.

questions.expl: Specific C1 inhibitor replacement is preferred perioperative prophylaxis for hereditary angioedema when available; FFP is an alternative when concentrate cannot be sourced.
questions.note: Some recalled answers say FFP only because the original option list may have omitted C1 inhibitor concentrate.

questions.stem: Sensory innervation of the cornea is by the

opts.why: CN III controls extraocular muscles and pupil function, not corneal sensation.
Facial nerve provides the blink reflex motor response, not its corneal afferent limb.
Trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, not sensory innervation of the cornea.

opts.t: Long ciliary nerves via nasociliary branch of V1

questions.expl: Corneal sensation runs with nasociliary (ophthalmic trigeminal V1) sensory fibres; facial VII supplies the efferent blink limb.

questions.stem: Local anaesthetic-induced myotoxicity is most likely to be associated with

opts.why: A one-off low-dose infiltration carries less muscle toxicity than prolonged bupivacaine exposure.
Ultrasound alone involves no tissue exposure to local anaesthetic drug.
Saline is not a myotoxic local anaesthetic.

opts.t: Prolonged bupivacaine exposure from an adductor canal catheter

questions.expl: Local anaesthetic myotoxicity is time and concentration dependent; prolonged infusion and bupivacaine exposure are recognised risk factors.

questions.stem: The minimum microshock current required to elicit ventricular fibrillation is

opts.why: An ampere is a massive macroshock current and far above intracardiac VF thresholds.
10 mA is 100-fold greater than the relevant 100 µA microshock scale.
100 mA is characteristic of dangerous external macroshock, not the minimum intracardiac current.

questions.expl: Microshock is direct intracardiac current and can cause VF at currents of order 100 µA; macroshock needs far larger current.
questions.note: Anki matched a MACROshock question and incorrectly suggested 100 mA; corrected for official microshock wording.

questions.stem: You give a dose of intravenous indocyanine green to facilitate videoangiography during cerebral aneurysm surgery. The displayed pulse oximetry (SpO2) and cerebral oxygen tissue saturation (SctO2) changes you expect to see are

A simultaneous SpO₂ rise is not the characteristic absorption artefact.

questions.expl: Indocyanine green absorbs red/near-infrared wavelengths, perturbing pulse oximetry and potentially increasing displayed regional cerebral oxygenation readings.

One week is far below the minimum supervised training period.

questions.stem: Of the following classes of medication for diabetes mellitus, the most likely to cause hypoglycaemia in the fasted patient are the

opts.why: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria and ketosis risk but do not usually provoke insulin-mediated fasting hypoglycaemia.
DPP-4 inhibitors are glucose-dependent insulin enhancers and seldom cause fasting hypoglycaemia alone.
Metformin suppresses hepatic glucose output without directly forcing insulin release, so intrinsic hypoglycaemia is uncommon.

questions.expl: Sulphonylureas continue stimulating insulin secretion during fasting and thus cause hypoglycaemia; the other listed oral agents have low intrinsic hypoglycaemia risk.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old ASA I patient develops ongoing seizures five minutes after receiving a brachial plexus block with ropivacaine. Of the following, the most suitable initial intravenous treatment is

opts.why: Calcium does not treat seizures from sodium-channel toxicity; consider it only for other indicated electrolyte/cardiac problems.
Giving more local anaesthetic worsens systemic toxicity and seizures.

opts.why: Phenytoin is not the preferred first-line anticonvulsant in LAST; benzodiazepines are recommended.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has the following pulmonary function test result. The most consistent diagnosis is

opts.why: PE may lower DLCO but generally does not produce this fixed restrictive spirometry pattern.
Asthma is primarily obstructive with variable expiratory airflow limitation, not parallel low volumes plus severe diffusion impairment.
Neuromuscular weakness can reduce volumes but does not explain the parenchymal diffusing-capacity pattern as well.

questions.expl: The sitting-specific recalled pulmonary function tests have reduced FEV1 and FVC (both approximately 68% predicted) with DLCO 46%, supporting a restrictive parenchymal process such as sarcoidosis; pulmonary vascular disease alone usually preserves volumes.
questions.note: Original FEV1/FVC results omitted; Brainscape supplied reconstructed values.

opts.why: Ulnar nerve continues in the medial cord distribution to medial arm/forearm and not the lateral-branch course shown.
Radial nerve is a posterior-cord terminal branch, not the terminal lateral-cord structure in this reconstruction.
Median nerve forms from two roots and does not branch as the depicted single musculocutaneous nerve.

questions.expl: The reconstructed brachial plexus illustration labels the musculocutaneous nerve separating from the lateral cord and coursing to the anterior arm.

questions.stem: You have been asked to anaesthetise a patient with a history of severe depression which has been well controlled on moclobemide. The most appropriate medications in combination with propofol are

opts.why: Pethidine has serotonergic activity with MAO inhibitors and metaraminol may pose sympathomimetic risk.
Tramadol is serotonergic and ephedrine indirectly releases catecholamines, creating serious interaction risk.
Ephedrine remains a poor indirect sympathomimetic choice, and fentanyl is more serotonergic than morphine.

questions.expl: Moclobemide inhibits MAO-A: avoid strongly serotonergic opioids and indirect sympathomimetics; morphine and direct-acting phenylephrine are safer choices.

questions.stem: Infection control management of patients with carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae (CPE) infection should include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.t: Contact precautions with gloves and gowns
opts.why: Contact isolation directly prevents transmission via hands and is required rather than excluded.
Single-room placement is a standard containment measure where feasible.

opts.t: Routine droplet precautions as the sole transmission precaution

opts.why: Dedicated patient equipment and toilet minimise environmental and contact transmission.

questions.expl: Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales spread largely by contact and contaminated environments. Contact precautions, dedicated equipment and patient placement are recommended; droplet precautions alone are not sufficient as the routine organism-specific strategy.
questions.note: The official stem asks EXCEPT. All three original reconstructed distractors were in fact appropriate CPE controls; replaced them to make the single-best-answer logic valid.

questions.stem: Blocking the sciatic nerve results in loss of function of all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Tibial division of sciatic controls plantar flexors via posterior leg muscles.
Sciatic innervates hamstrings that flex the knee.
Common fibular division of sciatic supplies foot dorsiflexors via deep fibular nerve.

questions.expl: Quadriceps/knee extension is femoral nerve (L2–4) function, while the sciatic nerve innervates hamstrings and most motor function below the knee.

questions.stem: Benztropine ameliorates the side effects of drugs that antagonize

opts.why: 5-HT₃ antagonists can cause nausea treatment effects but are not the cause of classic acute dystonia treated with benztropine.
H₁ blockade causes sedation/anticholinergic effects, not D₂-mediated extrapyramidal dystonia.
GABA-A antagonism causes excitation/seizures, rather than the dopaminergic-cholinergic imbalance of acute dystonia.

questions.expl: Benztropine is an antimuscarinic used to treat extrapyramidal dystonia from dopamine-D2 receptor blockade by antipsychotic/antiemetic drugs.

questions.stem: You are anaesthetising a 35-year-old woman undergoing a laparoscopic appendectomy. She uses a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (Mirena®) for contraception and you have used sugammadex for reversal of neuromuscular blockade at the end of the procedure. Your postoperative advice to her regarding contraception should state that

opts.why: Sugammadex can reduce reliability of steroidal contraception, including intrauterine hormonal devices.
Six months is far longer than the seven-day precaution recommended in product advice.

opts.t: Use additional contraception for seven days after sugammadex

opts.why: Twenty-four hours is shorter than the advised backup interval for hormonal contraception.

questions.expl: Sugammadex may bind steroidal contraception; advise extra non-hormonal protection for seven days, including users of hormonal systems, per product information.

questions.stem: You are resuscitating a 60 kg man in cardiac arrest secondary to severe hyperkalaemia. You decide to give intravenous sodium bicarbonate. Australian and New Zealand resuscitation guidelines state the initial dose of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate should be

opts.why: 30 mL supplies only 30 mmol, half of the recalled 1 mmol/kg dose for a 60 kg patient.
10 mL supplies only 10 mmol and is inadequate under the stated regimen.
120 mL delivers twice the 1 mmol/kg dose used in the recalled ANZCOR advice.

questions.expl: Older ANZCOR guidance for selected hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest described 1 mmol/kg 8.4% bicarbonate (1 mmol/mL), hence 60 mL for 60 kg.
questions.note: Bicarbonate is not routine for all arrests; calcium/insulin and hyperkalaemia protocols also apply.

questions.stem: Regarding healthcare research, the SQUIRE guidelines describe

opts.why: CONSORT governs randomised trial reports, not quality-improvement interventions.
PRISMA covers systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
STROBE concerns observational epidemiological studies, not formal reporting of QI work.

questions.expl: SQUIRE stands for Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence; it guides transparent reporting of QI interventions.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is administered an anaesthetic for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis. She is breastfeeding her six-week-old infant. During anaesthesia she receives the following drugs: propofol, fentanyl, sevoflurane, rocuronium, oxycodone, parecoxib, ondansetron, sugammadex and cefuroxime. The best advice regarding breastfeeding after anaesthesia is to

opts.t: Resume breastfeeding once awake and able to safely feed
Wait until all inhaled agent has fully left adipose tissue
opts.why: Complete elimination from fat is unnecessary; clinically meaningful milk exposure is generally very low.
Routine discarding for a day is not required after most standard anaesthetic agents.
A three-day interruption is excessive and not supported by standard breastfeeding guidance.

questions.expl: For most anaesthetic drugs, breastfeeding can resume once the mother is awake, stable and able to feed, with attention to opioid sedation and infant monitoring.

questions.stem: The most common cause of postoperative visual loss after spinal surgery is

opts.why: Retinal vein thrombosis is uncommon and does not dominate reported perioperative visual loss after spine surgery.
Retinal detachment is not the characteristic mechanism in prolonged prone procedures.
Angle-closure glaucoma is rare as the cause of reported postoperative visual loss in this setting.

questions.expl: Perioperative visual loss after prolonged spine surgery is most often associated with ischaemic optic neuropathy (posterior or anterior).

questions.stem: A baby is brought to the emergency department three days after a term home birth. It has not been feeding well and has had few wet nappies. The child is grey in appearance and femoral pulses are difficult to palpate. You note an enlarged liver and marked tachycardia. Pulse oximetry reveals saturations of 75% despite oxygen being administered. You suspect a duct-dependent circulation. The best initial management is

opts.why: A shocked cyanosed neonate with weak femoral pulses has an immediate threat to systemic perfusion, not an outpatient problem.

opts.t: Use a diuretic alone without ductal reopening
opts.why: Diuresis will not restore a closing ductus supplying systemic circulation.
Observation alone allows further ductal closure and deterioration in systemic perfusion.

opts.t: Start prostaglandin E₁ infusion (alprostadil) while resuscitating

questions.expl: A cyanosed shocked neonate with weak femorals and suspected duct-dependent systemic flow requires urgent PGE₁ to maintain/reopen the ductus plus ABC resuscitation.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of restless leg syndrome is experiencing significant agitation in the post- anaesthesia care unit. After excluding other precipitating causes, the best treatment of the agitation in this patient is

opts.why: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine and can exacerbate restless-leg symptoms.
Haloperidol's D₂ antagonism may worsen restless legs and akathisia.
Droperidol is another dopamine antagonist that can aggravate these movement symptoms.

questions.expl: Dopamine antagonists can worsen restless-leg symptoms; benzodiazepines may help immediate agitation while precipitating factors are addressed.

questions.stem: During trauma resuscitation in adults, contraindications to blind nasogastric tube insertion include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Major midfacial trauma risks passage of an NGT towards the cranial vault and is a contraindication.

opts.t: Clear rhinorrhoea suggestive of a CSF leak
opts.why: Possible CSF rhinorrhoea suggests skull-base disruption, so blind nasal instrumentation is unsafe.

opts.t: Isolated rib fracture without associated facial or skull injury

opts.why: Suspected basilar skull fracture is a classic reason to avoid blind nasal insertion.

questions.expl: The official question asks which condition is NOT a contraindication to blind nasogastric insertion. Skull-base fracture, major midfacial trauma and potential CSF rhinorrhoea raise concern for intracranial passage. Isolated rib fracture does not.
questions.note: Corrected a reversed EXCEPT answer in the preliminary answer bank; the previous draft incorrectly keyed skull-base fracture.

questions.stem: Cardiovascular effects of hyperthyroidism include

opts.why: Thyroid excess increases, rather than reduces, catecholamine sensitivity and chronotropy.
Hyperthyroidism usually produces hyperdynamic circulation, not a reduced blood volume state.
Resting tachycardia is common; bradycardia would be atypical without another cause or treatment.

questions.expl: Thyroid hormone increases beta-adrenergic responsiveness, heart rate and cardiac output; longstanding disease can cause arrhythmia and heart failure.

questions.stem: Effective pharmacotherapy options to support smoking cessation in the perioperative period include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Varenicline acts at nicotinic receptors and is an effective cessation treatment.
Bupropion has evidence for smoking cessation despite not being nicotine replacement.
Nicotine replacement reduces withdrawal symptoms and improves cessation success.

questions.expl: SSRIs have not shown reliable smoking cessation benefit; varenicline, bupropion and nicotine replacement are evidence-based treatments.

questions.stem: The main advantage of using norepinephrine (noradrenaline) over phenylephrine for the prevention of hypotension as a result of spinal anaesthesia for elective caesarean section is

opts.t: Greater uteroplacental blood flow by itself
opts.why: Preservation of uteroplacental flow is not established as a unique direct noradrenaline advantage over phenylephrine.
The main demonstrated difference is maternal heart rate, not a consistent reduction in fetal acidosis.
Apgar scores are generally comparable; this is not the principal clinical advantage.

questions.expl: Norepinephrine's modest beta activity preserves maternal heart rate better than pure alpha agonist phenylephrine in spinal-caesarean hypotension treatment.

questions.stem: The atmospheric lifetime of nitrous oxide (in years) is approximately

opts.why: Five hundred years greatly exceeds commonly quoted N₂O atmospheric persistence.
Five years is much shorter than the approximately century-long N₂O lifetime.
Fifteen years substantially underestimates nitrous oxide persistence in the atmosphere.

questions.expl: Nitrous oxide has a very long atmospheric residence time, usually estimated at around 114 years, contributing to climate impact.

questions.stem: The risk of a perioperative respiratory adverse event in a child is least likely to be increased by

opts.why: Recent URI causes airway inflammation and increases perioperative laryngospasm/bronchospasm risk.
Active asthma increases airway hyperreactivity during anaesthesia.
Passive cigarette smoke exposure is a recognised independent respiratory adverse-event risk.

questions.expl: Eczema alone is a weaker predictor of perioperative respiratory adverse events than symptomatic airway disease, a recent URI or passive smoking in the recalled options.
questions.note: Anki matched another scenario and suggested deep extubation, but specific 2021.1 Brainscape options support eczema.

questions.stem: In elderly patients without diabetes mellitus the use of aspirin in primary prevention of disease

opts.t: Marked reduction in stroke without bleeding
opts.why: ASPREE did not show the claimed stroke-prevention advantage without a bleeding tradeoff.

opts.t: Increased major bleeding without cardiovascular benefit in healthy older adults
Clear reduction in first MI without adverse effects
opts.why: Primary prevention did not produce an unambiguous first-MI benefit without harms.
All-cause mortality was not reduced by aspirin in the ASPREE population.

questions.expl: ASPREE found aspirin increased major haemorrhage without improving disability-free survival in healthy older adults.

questions.stem: You are involved in the care of a two-year-old child who has ingested a button battery in the last four hours. You would consider giving

opts.why: Blind home removal risks mucosal perforation and delays urgent specialist assessment.
Vomiting can cause further caustic injury and aspiration; it must not be induced.

opts.t: Give oral honey/sucralfate during urgent transfer, without delaying endoscopic removal

opts.why: Oesophageal batteries can cause severe tissue injury within hours; observation without urgent localisation/removal is unsafe.

questions.expl: In a child older than one year with recent suspected oesophageal button-battery ingestion, honey prehospital or sucralfate in hospital may reduce injury while urgent removal is arranged.

questions.stem: The most likely cause of hip adduction in a patient undergoing transurethral resection of a bladder tumour is

opts.why: The sciatic nerve is distant from the lateral bladder wall and cannot explain the diathermy-related obturator jerk.
Peroneal nerve injury causes distal leg deficits, not abrupt adductor spasm.
Femoral nerve controls quadriceps/knee extension, whereas obturator drives hip adduction.

questions.expl: Electrical stimulation of the obturator nerve adjacent to the lateral bladder wall causes forceful adductor contraction during TURBT.

questions.stem: In critically ill patients undergoing mechanical ventilation, energy dense enteral nutrition (1.5 kcal/mL/kg) compared to routine (1 kcal/mL/kg) enteral feeding provides

opts.why: TARGET did not establish an increase in ICU-free days with energy-dense feeds.
Duration of ventilation was not reliably shortened by the higher caloric-density strategy.
The trial did not show the major mortality benefit claimed for energy-dense feeding.

questions.expl: The TARGET trial found energy-dense enteral nutrition did not improve 90-day mortality in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.

questions.stem: Chronic recreational use of nitrous oxide may lead to

opts.t: Functional vitamin B₁₂ inactivation causing methionine synthase deficiency

opts.why: Choline excess is not the mechanism of N₂O-associated myeloneuropathy.
Iron deficiency does not explain the functional vitamin B₁₂ blockade caused by N₂O.
Vitamin K excess is unrelated to methionine synthase inhibition.

questions.expl: Chronic N₂O oxidises cobalamin, impairing methionine synthase and causing neurological myelopathy/neuropathy.

questions.stem: Risk factors for chronic postsurgical pain do NOT include

opts.why: Severe pain before surgery predicts chronic postsurgical pain.
Anxiety and psychological distress increase risk of persistent postsurgical pain.
Severe acute postoperative pain is a reproducible predictor of later chronic pain.

questions.expl: Chronic postsurgical pain risk is associated with pre-existing pain, distress and severe acute pain; higher education is not an established independent major risk factor.

questions.stem: A drug which is likely to slow the heart rate in a patient with a heart transplant is

opts.why: Phenylephrine may change blood pressure but transplanted denervation prevents the usual strong baroreflex bradycardia.
Digoxin's vagotonic AV-nodal effect is attenuated in a denervated transplanted heart.
Atropine blocks vagal input that is absent early after transplantation; it does not reliably slow heart rate.

questions.expl: Adenosine acts directly on A1 receptors in the transplanted heart and can profoundly slow AV conduction despite autonomic denervation; use cautiously because sensitivity may be exaggerated.
questions.note: The sitting-specific options recall adenosine; an alternate Anki card suggested esmolol but was not the same option set.

questions.stem: The following is an image from a focussed cardiac ultrasound in a patient with dyspnoea presenting for thoracic surgery. The diagnosis is

opts.why: Regional wall-motion abnormality is a contractility change, not a distinct anechoic pleural fluid collection.
A dilated ascending aorta is vascular enlargement, not free fluid separated by the diaphragm.
Pericardial tamponade is fluid around the heart with haemodynamic effects; the fluid here lies in pleural space.

questions.expl: The original recalled ultrasound shows an anechoic thoracic fluid space with compressed adjacent lung and visible diaphragm, consistent with pleural rather than pericardial effusion.

Thirty minutes concerns the period in which a unit should ordinarily be started, not finished.
Eight hours permits excessive warming and storage time compared with the four-hour limit.

opts.t: Within four hours of removal from controlled refrigeration

questions.expl: Packed RBC transfusion should ordinarily be completed within four hours after leaving controlled storage to reduce bacterial growth and haemolysis risk.

Spinal accessory nerve injury weakens trapezius and may cause winging.
Long thoracic nerve injury weakens serratus anterior and is a classic cause of winged scapula.

questions.stem: When commencing treatment of proximal deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolus, factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are preferred to dabigatran or warfarin because they do not require

opts.t: All DOACs require several days of LMWH
opts.why: Apixaban/rivaroxaban have oral loading regimens and do not need universal LMWH lead-in.

opts.t: Apixaban and rivaroxaban do not require initial parenteral heparin bridging
Dabigatran requires no initial parenteral treatment
opts.why: Dabigatran treatment of acute VTE follows several days of parenteral anticoagulation.
Warfarin takes days to become therapeutic and needs parenteral overlap initially.

questions.expl: Apixaban/rivaroxaban use front-loaded oral regimens for acute VTE. Dabigatran and edoxaban protocols require initial parenteral anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A neonate born by emergency caesarean section is limp, pale, has a weak grimace and weak cry, and a heart rate of 60 beats per minute. The Apgar Score is

opts.why: Seven would require considerably better tone, colour, respiration or rate than described.
Five is too high for the sum of HR 1, reflex 1, respiratory 1, tone 0 and colour 0.
Nine would imply near-normal newborn condition and cannot fit HR 60 and limp/pale findings.

questions.expl: Heart rate 60 gives 1, grimace 1, weak cry/poor breathing 1, limp tone 0 and pale appearance 0: total 3.
questions.note: A weak cry could be counted as respiration 1; as in recalled score 3.

questions.stem: Of the following, the LEAST likely cause of high anion gap metabolic acidosis is

opts.why: Lactate is an unmeasured anion that increases the calculated anion gap.
Salicylate accumulation causes a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (often alongside respiratory alkalosis).
Uraemic unmeasured sulphate, phosphate and other anions contribute to high-anion-gap acidosis.

questions.expl: Renal tubular acidosis usually causes normal-anion-gap hyperchloraemic acidosis, whereas lactate, uraemic organic anions and salicylates raise the gap.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a serum sodium of 110 mmol/L. A feature NOT consistent with a diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate antiduretic hormone (SIADH) is

opts.why: Clinical euvolaemia is expected in SIADH despite hyponatraemia.
Low serum osmolality is part of hypotonic hyponatraemia in SIADH.
Urine sodium is commonly above 30 mmol/L in euvolaemic SIADH with adequate intake.

questions.expl: SIADH produces inappropriately concentrated urine (>100 mOsm/kg) despite hypo-osmolality, with usual euvolaemia and urine sodium >30 mmol/L.

questions.stem: A patient with C6 tetraplegia is undergoing removal of bladder stones under general anaesthesia. The blood pressure rises to 166/88 mmHg. The appropriate response is to

opts.why: Continuing bladder stimulation aggravates the spinal sympathetic reflex and worsens dysreflexia.

opts.t: Allow sustained extreme hypertension without intervention
opts.why: Untreated severe hypertension risks stroke, haemorrhage and arrhythmia.

opts.t: Deepen anaesthesia and promptly treat autonomic dysreflexia

opts.why: An anticholinergic alone does not address sympathetic vasoconstriction or the noxious trigger.

questions.expl: Noxious stimuli below a high spinal cord lesion provoke autonomic dysreflexia; remove trigger, deepen anaesthesia and control marked hypertension.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought into the Emergency Department four hours after an accidental chemical exposure during crop spraying. His clinical signs include bradycardia, vomiting, diarrhoea, coughing, miosis and weakness. A drug which is NOT recommended during his resuscitation and treatment is

opts.why: Organophosphates inhibit cholinesterase and prolong, rather than accelerate, suxamethonium metabolism.

opts.t: Reversal by a beta blocker alone
opts.why: Beta blockade alone does not reverse muscarinic/nicotinic cholinergic poisoning.
Bradycardia, salivation, GI upset and bronchorrhoea are characteristic muscarinic effects.

questions.expl: Organophosphate pesticide exposure inhibits cholinesterases, producing cholinergic toxicity and prolonged suxamethonium paralysis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old previously healthy woman is four days post-caesarean section. You are asked to see her to manage her abdominal pain. Over the last two days she has had increasing abdominal pain, increasing abdominal distension, tachycardia and nausea. An abdominal x-ray shows a caecal diameter of 9 cm. After excluding mechanical obstruction, an appropriate management option is

opts.t: Repeat plain radiography alone as definitive diagnosis
opts.why: Plain-film monitoring alone does not reliably exclude mechanical obstruction or ischaemic complications.

opts.t: CT abdomen/pelvis to exclude obstruction and assess caecum

opts.why: Progressive distension and caecal enlargement require assessment, not unreviewed observation.
Emergency laparotomy without imaging or evidence of perforation/ischaemia is not first-line for an initially stable patient.

questions.expl: Post-caesarean distension and caecal dilatation suggest acute colonic pseudo-obstruction; imaging distinguishes mechanical obstruction/ischaemia before definitive treatment.
questions.note: Reconstructed stem might refer to excluded obstruction in other exams; here original report does not specify obstruction excluded.

questions.stem: The following ECG is consistent with

opts.why: WPW shows short PR/delta waves, not the reconstructed RVH voltage/axis pattern.
LVH causes greater left-sided voltage and often a leftward axis, not rightward RVH signs.

opts.t: Normal sinus rhythm without abnormal QRS pattern
opts.why: A normal ECG lacks the pathologic right-axis and right-precordial voltage changes.

questions.expl: The sitting-specific recalled ECG finding was right ventricular hypertrophy, suggested by rightward axis, dominant R waves in V1 and deep lateral S waves. A representative ECG is included for practice, not the original ANZCA tracing.
questions.note: ANZCA report does not reproduce the ECG; sitting-specific Brainscape recollection favours RVH. A prior generic Anki match suggested WPW and was rejected.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man suffers a hydrofluoric acid burn to 60% of his total body surface area in an industrial accident. An expected electrolyte disturbance is

opts.why: Magnesium is often chelated and decreases, not characteristically increases.
Fluoride complexes calcium, so elevated calcium is physiologically opposite.
Phosphate elevation is not the characteristic primary electrolyte effect of hydrofluoric acid injury.

questions.expl: Fluoride chelates calcium and magnesium and can cause profound life-threatening hypocalcaemia after hydrofluoric acid exposure.

questions.stem: The lung ultrasound finding most consistent with atelectasis is three or more

opts.why: A lung point is a highly specific sign of pneumothorax rather than interstitial/alveolar artefact.
Horizontal A-lines reflect aerated lung and do not indicate the described B-line pattern.
Absent lung pulse alone is nonspecific and does not represent three or more vertical artefacts.

questions.expl: Three or more vertical B-line artefacts between adjacent ribs indicate a pathologic interstitial/alveolar process and can accompany atelectasis, but they are not specific for atelectasis.
questions.note: 2021.1 recall lists three or more B-lines; the original wording is clinically nonspecific. The best ultrasound features of atelectatic consolidation include static air bronchograms and lung pulse.

questions.stem: If group A RhD negative fresh frozen plasma is not available for use in an A RhD positive patient, of the following your next best choice should be

opts.t: Group A plasma (RhD status not required for compatibility)

opts.why: Group O plasma often carries anti-A antibodies and may be incompatible with group A recipient erythrocytes.
Group B plasma contains anti-A and is incompatible with group A recipient RBCs.
Untested ABO-incompatible plasma risks intravascular haemolysis.

questions.expl: Plasma ABO compatibility is based on donor anti-A/anti-B antibodies. Group A (or AB) plasma is compatible with group A recipients; RhD status is generally not relevant for plasma.

questions.stem: Perioperative overheating is most likely to cause worsening of symptoms of

opts.why: Lambert–Eaton weakness is related to presynaptic calcium-channel dysfunction rather than Uhthoff's heat-sensitive CNS conduction.
Myasthenic transmission may worsen with illness, but the classic isolated heat-related conduction phenomenon is MS.
Duchenne is a dystrophinopathy and does not cause the characteristic temperature-dependent demyelinated conduction block.

questions.expl: Elevated body temperature transiently worsens conduction in demyelinated CNS pathways (Uhthoff phenomenon), aggravating MS symptoms.

questions.stem: A transhiatal oesophagectomy is performed via a

opts.t: Midline laparotomy and a left cervical incision, without thoracotomy

opts.why: A right thoracotomy converts the approach to a transthoracic oesophagectomy.
A thoracoabdominal incision is a different open thoracic approach.
Left thoracotomy alone does not correspond to the abdominal plus cervical transhiatal technique.

questions.expl: Transhiatal oesophagectomy uses abdominal dissection via hiatus with cervical anastomosis and avoids a formal thoracotomy.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman has a recent onset of dyspnoea and undergoes a right heart catheterisation, with results displayed below. Her pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 10 mmHg. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: Mitral regurgitation with haemodynamic pulmonary hypertension tends to elevate left atrial/wedge pressure.
Severe aortic stenosis causing pulmonary hypertension generally produces post-capillary elevated wedge pressure.
Mitral stenosis elevates left atrial pressure and PCWP, unlike the given normal wedge.

questions.expl: Reconstructed raised pulmonary artery pressures with PCWP 10 mmHg favour pre-capillary disease such as acute PE rather than elevated left atrial pressure.
questions.note: Original right-heart catheter values beyond PCWP were omitted; illustrative values supplied.

questions.stem: The modified Aldrete scoring system uses all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Consciousness is one of the five original Aldrete recovery components.
Circulation compares BP with baseline and contributes to the score.
Oxygenation or oxygen-saturation assessment is one of the recovery domains.

questions.expl: The original Aldrete score uses activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness and oxygenation; it does not include pain or nausea.

questions.stem: A woman with preeclampsia presents with a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg. An appropriate first line treatment to reduce the blood pressure is

opts.why: Warfarin is an anticoagulant and cannot treat hypertensive pre-eclampsia.
ACE inhibitors such as perindopril are contraindicated during pregnancy because of fetal toxicity.
Ergometrine may acutely increase blood pressure and is unsuitable as antihypertensive treatment.

questions.expl: Labetalol is a suitable agent for hypertension in pregnancy; ACE inhibitors are contraindicated and ergot agents raise BP.
questions.note: A BP 150/100 may not require acute IV antihypertensive therapy; thresholds vary by guideline.

questions.stem: The ANZCA Choosing Wisely recommendations advise avoiding all of the following EXCEPT

opts.t: Routine pre-operative tests in low-risk patients
opts.why: Avoiding routine unindicated preoperative tests is a core Choosing Wisely principle.
Imaging without a management-changing indication is low-value care.
Avoiding unnecessary RBC transfusion conserves resources and reduces transfusion harm.

opts.t: Epidural analgesia on maternal request in uncomplicated labour

questions.expl: Choosing Wisely discourages low-value routine investigations and interventions, not appropriate labour epidural analgesia requested after informed discussion.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with no past history of ischaemic heart disease is three days post-total hip replacement surgery. He has an episode of chest pain characteristic of angina which began at rest and lasted thirty minutes before resolving fully. There are no ECG changes. Six hours later there is a troponin rise above the 99th percentile upper reference limit. The diagnosis is

opts.why: Stable angina does not cause a new troponin rise fulfilling infarction criteria.
There are no diagnostic ST elevations in the described ECG, excluding STEMI classification.
Unstable angina has ischaemic symptoms without a diagnostic troponin rise.

questions.expl: Ischaemic chest symptoms and a troponin rise above the 99th percentile satisfy myocardial infarction criteria despite no ST elevation.
questions.note: An isolated postoperative troponin rise can also be termed MINS; symptoms make the NSTEMI classification plausible.

questions.stem: Consideration for same-day discharge in an ex-premature infant after orchidopexy for undescended testis would be suitable at a minimum postmenstrual age of

opts.t: Postmenstrual age around 54 weeks for an otherwise well ex-premature infant

opts.why: 44 weeks PMA is associated with substantially higher postoperative apnoea risk in former premature infants.
46 weeks still lies below the recalled conservative day-surgery discharge threshold.
40 weeks is essentially term-corrected age and too young for routine unmonitored discharge after anaesthesia.

questions.expl: Former preterm infants face postoperative apnoea risk; older ANZCA paediatric discharge guidance used approximately 54 weeks PMA as a threshold for selected day cases.
questions.note: Threshold is a historical recalled practice criterion; individual respiratory history and local policy matter.

questions.stem: The implemention of comprehensive multidisciplinary geriatric assessments in the peri-operative period has been shown to

opts.t: Reduced postoperative delirium and length of stay

opts.why: Comprehensive geriatric assessment is intended to improve care planning, not increase institutionalisation.
Trials generally report improved rather than increased delirium-related outcomes.
There is no established rise in perioperative mortality due to multidisciplinary geriatric assessment.
